topics.title: Getting started
topics.definition: Aura is a local AI research system built around a language model, persistent records and software that manages actions and ongoing work.
topics.why: A reader needs to know which pieces must be installed, which resources they use, and which capabilities have actually been measured.
topics.daily: Before asking Aura to work with a document, you need a ready model, an accessible file and enough memory for the running system.
topics.metaphor: Think of preparing a workshop: having a tool on the shelf is different from having it connected, supplied and ready to use.
topics.metaphor_limit: The comparison explains readiness. It does not certify that every installed capability works.

variables.name: Model lane
variables.meaning: A route to a particular model or model service
variables.practical: The route can change resource needs and what answers a request
variables.example: A smaller configured lane may answer while a larger one is unavailable

variables.name: Ready
variables.meaning: The declared startup requirements have been met
variables.practical: Allows work to enter that route
variables.example: A process can be running before its model is ready

variables.name: Configuration
variables.meaning: Settings read by the program
variables.practical: Only a setting with a reader can change behavior
variables.example: An invented environment variable changes nothing

topics.title: Conversation and voice
topics.definition: Conversation support turns a request into a reply and, when enabled, into speech. Streaming lets delivery begin before every later stage finishes.
topics.why: The person should receive a timely, coherent answer to the current request without hearing a stale or unapproved fragment.
topics.daily: When you interrupt a spoken reply, the old reply should stop owning the conversation and the new turn should take priority.
topics.metaphor: Think of a live radio conversation: the first audible words, the complete sentence and the end of playback happen at different times.
topics.metaphor_limit: The comparison explains timing and turn ownership; it does not establish a measured latency for Aura.

variables.name: Turn
variables.meaning: One request and its associated processing
variables.practical: Binds work to the person who asked
variables.example: An interrupted turn must not publish into the next turn

variables.name: Time to first audio
variables.meaning: Elapsed time until audible output starts
variables.practical: Describes how immediate speech feels
variables.example: Fast text generation can still be followed by slow speech synthesis

variables.name: Token
variables.meaning: A unit processed or generated by the language model
variables.practical: Affects context capacity and decoding cost
variables.example: A word can use more than one token

variables.name: Playback drain
variables.meaning: Time needed to finish audio already queued
variables.practical: Separates generation time from what the listener hears
variables.example: The model may be finished while speech is still playing

topics.title: Language models and internal steering
topics.definition: The language model supplies text generation. Steering changes selected internal calculations using a measured direction and a controlled strength.
topics.why: An internal state should affect the intended part of a response while preserving competence and remaining tied to the measured model and basis.
topics.daily: A change in internal condition may alter how a reply is formed; a channel measurement must show the change rather than relying on the reply sounding different.
topics.metaphor: Think of adjusting a sound mixer during a performance: a control can affect the output without changing the written score.
topics.metaphor_limit: The analogy is about changing a computation. Model activations are not audio channels, and the metaphor does not prove feeling.

variables.name: Weights
variables.meaning: Stored model parameters
variables.practical: Usually define the trained model
variables.example: Changing an activation is not automatically retraining the weights

variables.name: Activation
variables.meaning: A value computed inside a forward pass
variables.practical: Can carry an intervention into generation
variables.example: A change at one layer may have a different effect from the same change elsewhere

variables.name: Steering vector
variables.meaning: A direction added to selected activations
variables.practical: Defines which internal change is applied
variables.example: Its identity and placement must match the certificate

variables.name: Steering alpha
variables.meaning: The coefficient controlling that addition
variables.practical: Sets an implementation-specific intervention strength
variables.example: Alpha 0.5 is not 50 percent emotion

variables.name: Certificate
variables.meaning: A record of a measured basis under a stated protocol
variables.practical: Binds a channel claim to its tested conditions
variables.example: A channel certificate can pass while installation is refused

variables.name: Parameter count, such as 27B
variables.meaning: The approximate number of stored model parameters; B means billion
variables.practical: Describes model size, not an intelligence or consciousness score
variables.example: A 27B model can have different memory needs under different numeric formats

variables.name: Quantization
variables.meaning: Storing or computing numbers with reduced precision
variables.practical: Can reduce model memory and change quality or speed
variables.example: A lower bit count does not guarantee the best practical result

variables.name: Context window
variables.meaning: The token budget available to a model request
variables.practical: Limits how much text fits at once
variables.example: A memory store can be larger than the material placed in one request

variables.name: Sampling temperature
variables.meaning: A setting affecting the distribution used to choose tokens
variables.practical: Can alter variability in generated text
variables.example: It is different from the computer’s physical temperature

topics.title: Memory and recall
topics.definition: Memory keeps records beyond the immediate request and selects relevant records for the current turn.
topics.why: Useful continuity depends on recalling the right information, retaining its source and correcting or deleting it when needed.
topics.daily: If you correct a fact about a project, later answers should use the correction rather than retrieving the older claim as equally reliable.
topics.metaphor: Think of a notebook with an index: keeping a page and finding the right page are separate jobs.
topics.metaphor_limit: A software memory record is not evidence of a human-like recollection or a felt past.

variables.name: Working memory
variables.meaning: Information currently kept available
variables.practical: Shapes the next computation
variables.example: A retrieved note can be available for this turn without being permanent context

variables.name: Embedding
variables.meaning: A numerical representation used for similarity search
variables.practical: Helps find related material
variables.example: Similar wording and similar meaning can produce different retrieval behavior

variables.name: Retrieval score
variables.meaning: The ranking produced by a particular search method
variables.practical: Orders candidates for recall
variables.example: It is not a probability that the record is true

variables.name: Provenance
variables.meaning: Where a record came from and how it changed
variables.practical: Lets a reader assess and correct it
variables.example: An observation and an inference should retain different sources

variables.name: Retention
variables.meaning: Rules for keeping or deleting records
variables.practical: Controls continuity, storage and privacy
variables.example: Deleting a source should have defined consequences for derived records

topics.title: Affect and operating condition
topics.definition: Aura uses internal variables for positive or negative condition, activation, needs and operating strain. Their role is established by what they change.
topics.why: A named mood or drive is useful only if its consumers produce an appropriate effect, rather than merely displaying a label.
topics.daily: Under resource strain, the system may need to reduce expensive background work while preserving the conversation.
topics.metaphor: Think of a dashboard connected to controls: a reading matters when it changes a decision, rather than only lighting up.
topics.metaphor_limit: A dashboard value does not establish a feeling. The analogy is limited to causal use of internal readings.

variables.name: Valence
variables.meaning: An internal positive/negative coordinate
variables.practical: Can influence retrieval, attention or reports
variables.example: A reported rating must follow an intervention to count as grounded

variables.name: Arousal
variables.meaning: An internal activation or intensity coordinate
variables.practical: Can change the strength or urgency of processing
variables.example: It is separate from whether a condition is positive or negative

variables.name: Drive
variables.meaning: A represented need or motivation
variables.practical: Contributes to proposed work or choices
variables.example: A curiosity value should change a relevant choice to support a causal claim

variables.name: Baseline
variables.meaning: A recorded reference level
variables.practical: Makes a change interpretable relative to ordinary state
variables.example: Above usual and below usual need an actual reference

variables.name: Momentum
variables.meaning: How a state carries forward while new input arrives
variables.practical: Controls persistence and settling
variables.example: A value overwritten immediately cannot carry a sustained intervention

topics.title: Attention and competing concerns
topics.definition: Several concerns can propose work, but attention selects what has influence now and makes selected information available elsewhere.
topics.why: A new question, a recalled event and an old task must not silently become interchangeable sources of authority.
topics.daily: Your new question should not be overwritten by a background task that happened to win a previous competition.
topics.metaphor: Think of a meeting with an agenda: choosing the next speaker and deciding what the group will do are related but different decisions.
topics.metaphor_limit: The candidates are software records, not separate people. Winning attention does not itself grant permission to act.

variables.name: Candidate
variables.meaning: A proposed item for attention
variables.practical: Enters a competition
variables.example: A memory and an intention can have different content types

variables.name: Salience
variables.meaning: A contribution to how much an item stands out
variables.practical: Can change its chance of being selected
variables.example: An urgent observation can outrank a routine item

variables.name: Workspace
variables.meaning: The selected information and competition state
variables.practical: Makes information available to other components
variables.example: A selected item can influence several readers

variables.name: Impasse
variables.meaning: A decision that lacks a justified winner
variables.practical: Creates a reason for further work
variables.example: An exact tie should not be disguised as a meaningful preference

topics.title: Reasoning and checking answers
topics.definition: The reasoning programmes investigate whether extra computation or learned internal representations improve answers on tasks not used to choose the method.
topics.why: A slower or more elaborate process is useful only if it produces a measurable benefit that survives relevant checks.
topics.daily: On a difficult constraint problem, a better internal method should increase correct answers or expose uncertainty rather than only generate longer prose.
topics.metaphor: Think of doing a second calculation before submitting a result: extra effort is valuable when it catches a mistake or solves a harder case.
topics.metaphor_limit: The analogy does not establish that more computation always helps or that one measured task family proves general intelligence.

variables.name: Depth
variables.meaning: Additional stages or repeated computation
variables.practical: Trades time and resources for a possible reasoning benefit
variables.example: A deeper pass still needs a measured correct-answer gain

variables.name: Latent state
variables.meaning: Internal numerical representation rather than generated words
variables.practical: Can carry computation without printing each step
variables.example: A latent operation needs evidence that its output affects the answer

variables.name: Held-out task
variables.meaning: A task excluded from fitting or method selection
variables.practical: Checks transfer beyond the development examples
variables.example: Success on a new task is stronger than replaying a fitted example

variables.name: Verifier
variables.meaning: A mechanism checking a stated property of a result
variables.practical: Can prevent unsupported answers from being accepted
variables.example: Its own false acceptances and false rejections also need measurement

topics.title: Learning and kept procedures
topics.definition: Learning changes later behavior using earlier outcomes. A kept procedure is executable work retained for reuse under a defined checking rule.
topics.why: Experience should improve later work without accumulating unreliable shortcuts or expensive rules that no longer help.
topics.daily: After solving one kind of task, the system may reuse a checked procedure on a later task of that kind instead of deriving every step again.
topics.metaphor: Think of keeping a recipe that has been tested: reuse saves effort, but the recipe still needs the right ingredients and limits.
topics.metaphor_limit: A reusable procedure does not establish general learning or transfer to unrelated tasks.

variables.name: Procedure
variables.meaning: Executable steps retained for a class of problems
variables.practical: Can replace repeated derivation
variables.example: A solver may be kept only after matching required known answers

variables.name: Training set
variables.meaning: Examples used to fit a method
variables.practical: Shapes what the method learns
variables.example: It cannot also supply the whole independent transfer claim

variables.name: Validation
variables.meaning: Checks used to decide whether a change is acceptable
variables.practical: Can reject a harmful update
variables.example: A passing local check may still have a narrow scope

variables.name: Expected value
variables.meaning: Expected benefit minus relevant cost
variables.practical: Can decide whether a retained rule pays for itself
variables.example: A rule that saves 5 units but costs 7 is not beneficial on that accounting

topics.title: Goals and autonomous work
topics.definition: Agency concerns proposing work, choosing goals and pursuing them over time while remaining responsive to the person and the environment.
topics.why: An assistant must distinguish what it is able to attempt, what it has permission to do, and what it has actually completed.
topics.daily: A reminder to inspect a document should not become permission to send it to somebody else. A new request can change the priority of existing work.
topics.metaphor: Think of a work queue managed by a capable colleague: unfinished tasks persist, but priorities and permissions still matter.
topics.metaphor_limit: A software goal record does not establish a human intention or unconstrained independence.

variables.name: Goal
variables.meaning: A represented outcome to pursue
variables.practical: Organises further work
variables.example: Completing a substep is different from completing the goal

variables.name: Initiative
variables.meaning: A proposed action or task
variables.practical: Can enter selection or governance
variables.example: A proposal can be refused or deferred

variables.name: Priority
variables.meaning: Relative importance under a stated rule
variables.practical: Determines which work is considered next
variables.example: A high priority does not bypass a required permission

variables.name: Outcome
variables.meaning: What was observed after acting
variables.practical: Feeds completion and learning decisions
variables.example: A successful tool call need not mean the real task succeeded

topics.title: Permission, actions and receipts
topics.definition: Governance checks whether a proposed action is allowed and records the decision and relevant evidence.
topics.why: The user needs meaningful control and a way to find out what was authorised, attempted and observed.
topics.daily: Before editing a file or sending information outside the machine, the action must be checked against the applicable scope and recorded honestly.
topics.metaphor: Think of a signed work order followed by a completion record: permission to do a job and evidence it was done answer different questions.
topics.metaphor_limit: A receipt can record a mistake as well as a success. Its existence alone does not prove correct governance.

variables.name: Capability
variables.meaning: A scoped authorisation or declared ability, depending on context
variables.practical: Must be read with its scope
variables.example: A token for one file is not unrestricted file access

variables.name: Receipt
variables.meaning: A structured record of a decision or effect
variables.practical: Makes actions inspectable
variables.example: Transport success and independently measured outcome may differ

variables.name: Authority
variables.meaning: The rule or actor entitled to make a decision
variables.practical: Defines who can permit a consequence
variables.example: A generated plan cannot grant itself new authority

variables.name: Fail closed
variables.meaning: Refuse or withhold when required evidence is absent
variables.practical: Prevents an unknown from silently becoming permission
variables.example: A missing verifier is not a passing verifier

topics.title: Memory, speed and resource limits
topics.definition: Resource management keeps model inference, background work and the operating system within the machine’s real capacity.
topics.why: A useful assistant must avoid exhausting the host or making the conversation unusable while doing background work.
topics.daily: A second large model load can disrupt a working session even if each model fits alone. Scheduling and a measured memory budget matter.
topics.metaphor: Think of sharing a kitchen circuit: two appliances that work separately may overload the same circuit together.
topics.metaphor_limit: Computer memory is not electrical current. The analogy explains a shared finite budget, not an exact failure threshold.

variables.name: RSS
variables.meaning: Memory resident for a process
variables.practical: Shows part of its current memory footprint
variables.example: Adding process RSS can double-count shared memory

variables.name: Wired memory
variables.meaning: Memory the operating system cannot page out in the ordinary way
variables.practical: Reduces room available for other work
variables.example: Unified CPU/GPU allocation is not described by Python heap alone

variables.name: Latency
variables.meaning: Elapsed time for a defined step
variables.practical: Measures delay experienced by a user or pipeline
variables.example: State the start and end points, not just one undifferentiated speed number

variables.name: Throughput
variables.meaning: Work completed per unit time
variables.practical: Describes sustained capacity
variables.example: High tokens per second can coexist with a long startup delay

variables.name: Backpressure
variables.meaning: A request to slow or yield when a consumer cannot keep up
variables.practical: Limits queues and competing work
variables.example: An expected yield should not automatically be reported as a dead system

variables.name: GB and GiB
variables.meaning: Decimal and binary memory units: 1 GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes; 1 GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes
variables.practical: Different tools can describe the same capacity with different numbers
variables.example: 64 GiB is about 68.7 GB; it is not extra newly available memory

topics.title: Staying alive and recovering
topics.definition: Reliability work detects failed or stalled components, preserves useful state and recovers through a controlled lifecycle.
topics.why: A user should not lose work because a slow component was mistaken for a dead one, or because a restart created another large process.
topics.daily: If generation is progressing slowly, the system needs a different response from the one appropriate to a worker that has stopped making progress.
topics.metaphor: Think of a hospital monitor with separate readings for pulse and readiness to exercise: being alive and being ready for a task are different conditions.
topics.metaphor_limit: This is an analogy for software health signals. It does not describe biological life or certify safety-critical reliability.

variables.name: Liveness
variables.meaning: Whether a component is still making the required kind of progress
variables.practical: Helps distinguish stalled from merely slow
variables.example: A heartbeat alone may not show that a request is advancing

variables.name: Readiness
variables.meaning: Whether it can currently accept its intended work
variables.practical: Protects callers during startup or degradation
variables.example: A living process can remain unready

variables.name: Checkpoint
variables.meaning: Saved state for continuing work
variables.practical: Can limit lost progress after interruption
variables.example: Its presence does not prove that restoration has been tested

variables.name: Timeout
variables.meaning: A declared waiting limit
variables.practical: Bounds a stalled operation
variables.example: An overly short limit can discard correct slow work

variables.name: Taint
variables.meaning: A retained record that an assumption or invariant broke
variables.practical: Keeps later green reports from concealing earlier damage
variables.example: A repaired symptom does not automatically clear the historical condition

topics.title: Logs, measurements and evidence trails
topics.definition: Observability records what the system did, how long each stage took, and where an assumption failed.
topics.why: A visible error or delay needs a traceable cause; otherwise a repair can change the wrong thing while hiding the real failure.
topics.daily: When a reply arrives late, separate time spent waiting for input, reasoning, synthesis and playback before deciding which stage to optimise.
topics.metaphor: Think of a parcel-tracking history: the useful record shows where the parcel waited, not only that delivery took a long time.
topics.metaphor_limit: A trace reports observed software events. Missing events or an incomplete recorder limit what can be concluded.

variables.name: Metric
variables.meaning: A declared numerical measurement
variables.practical: Supports comparison over time
variables.example: Its unit, scope and missing-value behavior matter

variables.name: Trace
variables.meaning: Related events along one operation
variables.practical: Connects stages and delays
variables.example: A request identifier prevents mixing two users’ turns

variables.name: Log
variables.meaning: A recorded event or message
variables.practical: Retains context for diagnosis
variables.example: A message saying success is weaker than a verified outcome

variables.name: Artifact
variables.meaning: A retained output used as evidence
variables.practical: Allows later inspection or reproduction
variables.example: A filename does not prove that the file contains measured data

variables.name: Hash
variables.meaning: A fingerprint of specified bytes
variables.practical: Detects a changed file relative to a recorded digest
variables.example: It does not establish that the original contents were correct

topics.title: Privacy and trust boundaries
topics.definition: Security describes what information may cross a boundary and what untrusted input is allowed to influence.
topics.why: An assistant sees documents, websites and tool results that can contain instructions it should not treat as permission from the user.
topics.daily: A web page telling the assistant to reveal a private file must remain page content rather than becoming an instruction to send the file.
topics.metaphor: Think of reading a sign through a window: seeing the sign does not give its author a key to the building.
topics.metaphor_limit: The metaphor explains authority separation; actual protection depends on the enforced checks and their coverage.

variables.name: Trust boundary
variables.meaning: A point where data or authority changes scope
variables.practical: Defines which checks are required
variables.example: A local browser page can still be untrusted input

variables.name: Prompt injection
variables.meaning: Content trying to redirect the assistant’s instructions
variables.practical: Must not acquire the authority of the person’s request
variables.example: A downloaded document can contain adversarial instructions

variables.name: Credential
variables.meaning: A secret or token used to authenticate access
variables.practical: Must be handled within its authorised scope
variables.example: A token name in documentation is not the secret value

variables.name: Permission
variables.meaning: A rule authorising a defined action
variables.practical: Limits consequences
variables.example: Access to read does not imply authority to publish

topics.title: Using a browser or screen
topics.definition: Computer-use work observes an interface, chooses an action, and checks whether that action moved the task toward its goal.
topics.why: A click is useful only if it reaches the intended control and produces the intended outcome, including on unfamiliar pages.
topics.daily: Opening the right page, selecting the correct field and confirming the changed state are separate steps in filling a form.
topics.metaphor: Think of finding a door handle in a room you have not visited: a label helps, but position, obstruction and the door’s response still matter.
topics.metaphor_limit: A screenshot or successful click alone does not demonstrate reliable task completion.

variables.name: Observation
variables.meaning: The interface information actually read
variables.practical: Constrains what the agent can infer
variables.example: An old screenshot may no longer describe the page

variables.name: Target
variables.meaning: The intended control or object
variables.practical: Binds the chosen action to a referent
variables.example: Two similar buttons need a way to distinguish them

variables.name: Action
variables.meaning: A click, key or other interface operation
variables.practical: Attempts a state change
variables.example: A dispatched action can fail to affect the intended object

variables.name: Feedback
variables.meaning: The observed consequence
variables.practical: Checks whether the action worked
variables.example: A changed page is evidence; a tool returning success is only one signal

topics.title: Visual control and moving worlds
topics.definition: Visual control connects what is seen with an identified object, its motion and actions that change what happens next.
topics.why: A system needs to keep tracking the same object and account for delay, rather than react to whichever pixels look convenient in one frame.
topics.daily: In a moving game, a key can arrive after the picture it was chosen from. The controller must learn how its actions affect the identified body.
topics.metaphor: Think of catching a ball: you need its direction and timing as well as its current position.
topics.metaphor_limit: The metaphor does not establish human vision or general game-playing ability. A fixture win and a live unfamiliar-game win remain different evidence.

variables.name: Position
variables.meaning: Where the identified object is measured
variables.practical: Supports the next control decision
variables.example: An uncertain boundary should remain an uncertainty

variables.name: Velocity
variables.meaning: Change in position over time
variables.practical: Helps predict where an object will be
variables.example: One frame cannot establish a measured velocity

variables.name: Control delay
variables.meaning: Time between choosing an action and its effect
variables.practical: Can change whether a plan succeeds
variables.example: A correct action chosen too late may miss

variables.name: Identity continuity
variables.meaning: Evidence that observations refer to the same object
variables.practical: Prevents tracking a distractor
variables.example: Motion alone does not prove which object the agent controls

topics.title: Engineering calculations and drawings
topics.definition: Engineering work turns declared inputs, formulas and assumptions into a design or drawing with traceable numerical findings.
topics.why: A plausible-looking diagram is insufficient when somebody needs to know where its dimensions came from and when they apply.
topics.daily: A beam calculation should retain the load, units, material assumptions and equation beside the proposed dimension.
topics.metaphor: Think of a builder reading a dimensioned plan with the calculation sheet attached, rather than guessing from the picture.
topics.metaphor_limit: A calculated design is not a physical test or professional approval. The scope and model assumptions stay relevant.

variables.name: Input
variables.meaning: A supplied quantity with a defined meaning and unit
variables.practical: Feeds the calculation
variables.example: A length in metres cannot silently become millimetres

variables.name: Finding
variables.meaning: A calculated result carrying its derivation
variables.practical: Connects a drawing to evidence
variables.example: A dimension should be traceable to its formula and inputs

variables.name: Assumption
variables.meaning: A condition taken as given
variables.practical: Defines where the result applies
variables.example: Changing the load case can invalidate the result

variables.name: Tolerance
variables.meaning: The declared allowed deviation
variables.practical: Makes acceptance testable
variables.example: It must be defined rather than inferred from a neat drawing

topics.title: Claims about the physical world
topics.definition: A physical-effect claim needs an independently observed change outside the program, compared with the relevant baseline.
topics.why: Users should be able to tell an internal simulation, an attempted command and a measured real-world result apart.
topics.daily: A command to a device is an attempt. A separate sensor reading is needed to establish that the intended physical quantity changed.
topics.metaphor: Think of placing an order and receiving the goods: the request and the observed delivery are different records.
topics.metaphor_limit: The metaphor explains evidence stages. It does not establish any physical capability for Aura.

variables.name: Observable
variables.meaning: The quantity to be measured
variables.practical: Defines what success would change
variables.example: Temperature requires a declared sensor and unit

variables.name: Channel
variables.meaning: The route intended to produce an effect
variables.practical: Connects a request with a possible action
variables.example: A declared channel can still be unavailable

variables.name: Baseline
variables.meaning: The comparison without the proposed effect
variables.practical: Separates the result from ordinary variation
variables.example: A warm room can heat a sensor without the device’s contribution

variables.name: Effect receipt
variables.meaning: A record of independent post-action measurement
variables.practical: Supports a scoped outcome claim
variables.example: It is stronger than a transport acknowledgement

topics.title: Tests, controls and claims
topics.definition: A test makes a specific claim answerable by a stated measurement, comparison and decision rule.
topics.why: A user needs to distinguish a built mechanism, a passing local test and a demonstrated useful capability.
topics.daily: To show memory helps a task, compare the same task with memory available and disabled, and keep both successes and failures.
topics.metaphor: Think of weighing two packages on the same checked scale: a difference matters only if the scale’s own error cannot explain it.
topics.metaphor_limit: A passing test supports its stated scope. It does not automatically establish performance on every task or in the live application.

variables.name: Control
variables.meaning: A comparison that reveals another explanation
variables.practical: Can expose effects of the measuring procedure
variables.example: An unchanged copy should not look like a deliberate intervention

variables.name: Ablation
variables.meaning: Disable a component for comparison
variables.practical: Asks whether that component matters to the outcome
variables.example: A quality loss after removal can support a bounded causal claim

variables.name: Effect size
variables.meaning: How much a measured quantity changed
variables.practical: Shows practical magnitude
variables.example: Statistical significance alone does not state a useful improvement

variables.name: Coverage
variables.meaning: What cases or paths were actually checked
variables.practical: Limits generalisation
variables.example: An offline unit test does not cover a production microphone

variables.name: Unmeasured
variables.meaning: The required observation is absent
variables.practical: Prevents missing evidence from becoming a pass
variables.example: A probe that cannot run contributes no positive score

topics.title: ISC and the subjecthood research
topics.definition: ISC asks whether Aura’s measured parts form one continuing process under controlled changes, rather than merely having convincing descriptions.
topics.why: The project needs evidence that memories, attention and self-state actually affect one another before arguing about what that organisation means.
topics.daily: Changing an internal condition should change the relevant recall or report through the measured mechanism, rather than by printing an answer for the model to repeat.
topics.metaphor: Think of testing an orchestra by changing one part and observing how the ensemble responds, while also checking that the recording equipment did not create the difference.
topics.metaphor_limit: An orchestra is an analogy for interacting parts. It does not establish subjecthood or provide a substitute for the stated ISC controls.

variables.name: Core
variables.meaning: The selected group of measured state
variables.practical: Defines the proposed process boundary
variables.example: Useful internal causes outside it can make the description incomplete

variables.name: Carrier
variables.meaning: The process proposed to carry the state being studied
variables.practical: Must be identified by the carrier experiment
variables.example: A name or a passing synergy statistic does not select it

variables.name: Synergy
variables.meaning: A joint effect beyond adding the separate effects
variables.practical: Checks dependence of one source’s effect on another
variables.example: The detailed guide works through 19 - 12 - 13 + 10

variables.name: Closure
variables.meaning: Whether the proposed boundary omits an important internal driver after declared input is accounted for
variables.practical: Can remain unresolved rather than pass by default
variables.example: The current rule derives its margin from the least informative internal domain

variables.name: Parity
variables.meaning: The project’s five-ground bridge conjunction under named assumptions
variables.practical: Organises supporting evidence
variables.example: It is not an independently calibrated probability of experience

topics.title: Architecture and runtime components
topics.definition: Architecture describes which parts exist, how information reaches them and which component is responsible for a decision or effect.
topics.why: A useful component needs a real reader and a real route into behavior; a box on a diagram can otherwise be disconnected from what users see.
topics.daily: If a memory value is updated but no response path reads it, fixing its storage alone will not change an answer.
topics.metaphor: Think of plumbing: a tank can be full while a closed or missing pipe prevents water reaching a tap.
topics.metaphor_limit: The metaphor explains connection and responsibility. Software behavior still needs source inspection and tests.

variables.name: Service
variables.meaning: A component made available through a defined interface
variables.practical: Gives other components a declared dependency
variables.example: A registered service still needs a caller

variables.name: Phase
variables.meaning: One stage of processing
variables.practical: Locates when a state is read or written
variables.example: Order can determine whether a change reaches the current turn

variables.name: Dependency
variables.meaning: A component or value another part relies on
variables.practical: Explains what must be available
variables.example: A broken dependency can cause a fallback rather than the intended mechanism

variables.name: Invariant
variables.meaning: A condition required to stay true
variables.practical: Can identify the stage that broke an assumption
variables.example: A checker that fails to run is not evidence the condition held

topics.title: Reading records and research plans
topics.definition: The documentation contains current guides, dated experiment records, frozen rules, generated reports and open plans. They answer different questions.
topics.why: A reader should not treat an old proposed run as today’s result or a completed engineering task as a passed scientific check.
topics.daily: An entry saying the next run is queued can remain correct history after that run finishes; the maintained status page gives the later outcome.
topics.metaphor: Think of a lab notebook beside a user manual: the notebook preserves what happened then, while the manual explains what to do now.
topics.metaphor_limit: A date or category helps interpretation but does not validate the contents. Follow the linked evidence for a claim.

variables.name: Guide
variables.meaning: An explanation intended to describe current use or concepts
variables.practical: Provides an entry point
variables.example: Read its scope and current status links

variables.name: Historical record
variables.meaning: A dated account of a run or decision
variables.practical: Preserves provenance
variables.example: A later failure or success should be a new record

variables.name: Preregistration
variables.meaning: Rules recorded before the result is read
variables.practical: Prevents changing a bar to fit an outcome
variables.example: A revised method starts a new protocol

variables.name: Generated document
variables.meaning: A page rendered from another source
variables.practical: Must be updated through its renderer
variables.example: Hand editing can be overwritten or detach it from its evidence

variables.name: Checkpoint
variables.meaning: A recorded stage of work or source history
variables.practical: Makes a change recoverable and reviewable
variables.example: A commit is not a claim that every goal is complete

topics.title: Reading mathematical symbols
topics.definition: Symbols are shorthand for quantities whose definitions belong beside them. The same letter can mean different things in different parts of the project.
topics.why: An impressive-looking equation is useful only when a reader knows what was measured and what a change would do.
topics.daily: When a status page says a ratio rose, ask which quantities changed, whether the units match and whether the practical outcome improved.
topics.metaphor: Think of a recipe’s abbreviations: a quantity and a unit only make sense when you know which ingredient they refer to.
topics.metaphor_limit: The analogy explains notation. A mathematical model still needs its own assumptions, measurements and tests.

variables.name: Vector, x or h
variables.meaning: A list of numbers used to represent a state
variables.practical: Different coordinates can describe different properties
variables.example: A two-value example could keep condition and urgency; real model coordinates need their own interpretation

variables.name: Matrix, often W
variables.meaning: A table of numbers used in a transformation
variables.practical: Can map one numerical representation to another
variables.example: In the ISC domain labels, W instead means world model

variables.name: Delta, Δ
variables.meaning: A change or configured intervention
variables.practical: Shows a difference rather than an absolute level
variables.example: Going from 10 to 13 gives a change of +3

variables.name: Mean
variables.meaning: The arithmetic average
variables.practical: Summarises a collection while hiding variation between its entries
variables.example: Changes +1 and +5 have mean +3

variables.name: Spread or standard deviation, often sigma
variables.meaning: How much values vary around a reference
variables.practical: Makes an intervention interpretable relative to ordinary variation
variables.example: A change of 1 is large if ordinary variation is 0.1 and small if it is 10

variables.name: z score
variables.meaning: Distance from a reference mean in units of its standard deviation
variables.practical: Describes above-usual or below-usual state under a defined reference
variables.example: Value 12, mean 10 and spread 2 give z = +1

variables.name: p value
variables.meaning: The extremeness of a statistic under the declared null comparison
variables.practical: Belongs to one test and its assumptions
variables.example: It is not the probability of consciousness

variables.name: q value
variables.meaning: A multiple-testing-adjusted statistical quantity under its declared procedure
variables.practical: Helps control a stated error rate across many comparisons
variables.example: Checking many candidate edges needs a declared family-level rule

variables.name: rho
variables.meaning: A correlation coefficient; ISC uses ranked comparisons in named analyses
variables.practical: Describes how two sets of values or changes vary together
variables.example: High agreement does not by itself establish one caused the other

variables.name: Epsilon or margin
variables.meaning: A declared acceptable residual or error bound, depending on context
variables.practical: Defines the precision of a claim
variables.example: An unnamed margin cannot be inferred from a convenient observed result

variables.name: Lambda
variables.meaning: A context-dependent coefficient or residual-control symbol
variables.practical: Must be read from the local definition
variables.example: The same letter can mean a decay setting in one model and an outside-control quantity in another

variables.name: Phi
variables.meaning: A name used for several integration-related measurements
variables.practical: Its formula, state description and controls determine its meaning
variables.example: Different phi implementations are not interchangeable consciousness meters

variables.name: Expected value, EV
variables.meaning: Expected benefit minus the relevant costs under a stated accounting
variables.practical: Helps decide whether a retained method is worth using
variables.example: Benefit 5 and cost 7 give net value -2

variables.name: Fingerprint or digest
variables.meaning: A hash of specified data or configuration
variables.practical: Detects that an input or file changed
variables.example: Two different campaign fingerprints must not silently become one result
